title: Singapore Opposition MP Opposes Temasek Funds for Air India as Losses Cross $2 Billion
excerpt: Workers Party lawmaker Kenneth Tiong has filed a parliamentary question after Air India reportedly sought $1.5 billion in fresh equity from Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines.
body:
• Singapore opposition lawmaker Kenneth Tiong has publicly opposed the use of Temasek funds to support Air India through Singapore Airlines, filing a parliamentary question for September 8.
  • Air India is reportedly seeking $1.5 billion in fresh equity from majority owner Tata Sons and minority stakeholder Singapore Airlines.
  • Singapore Airlines recorded $945 million in shared losses from its 25.1% stake in Air India during FY2025/26, contributing to a 56% decline in the carrier's net profit.
  • Air India posted over ₹22,000 crore in losses during FY26, hit by Pakistan's airspace ban, the Iran-US conflict, and the fallout from a fatal crash in June 2025.

Singapore Airlines' investment in Air India has drawn political scrutiny in the city-state after an opposition lawmaker publicly opposed the use of government-linked funds to support the loss-making Indian carrier. The comments mark the first time the commercial investment has become a matter of political debate in Singapore's parliament.

Kenneth Tiong, a member of parliament from the opposition Workers' Party, said in a social media post on Wednesday that because Singapore Airlines owns about 25% of Air India and state investor Temasek Holdings in turn owns a majority stake in the Singapore carrier, the request for fresh capital was "not only a question for private shareholders."

"No one, least of all Singaporeans, owes Air India a living. I will not support, nor expect, any future use of Temasek's funds to prop up Air India via Singapore Airlines. If Singapore Airlines wants to continue its bet on Air India, it should do so on its own two feet, and not on Temasek."

— Kenneth Tiong, Workers' Party MP, Singapore

Air India Seeks $1.5 Billion in Fresh Capital

The political pressure comes as Air India has reportedly asked owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines for $1.5 billion in fresh equity, according to Reuters. The demand for additional funding follows the airline's losses widening to over ₹22,000 crore in FY26, more than double the previous year. Air India and its budget arm Air India Express posted combined losses of $2.33 billion in the year to March 2026.

Singapore Airlines said on Thursday that its board will "carefully consider" any requests for additional capital from Air India, taking into consideration the group's other capital requirements and the Indian carrier's business strategy. The airline did not disclose a fixed investment limit.

The carrying value of SIA's 25.1% stake in Air India fell to $1.13 billion as of March 31, 2026, from $2.02 billion a year earlier. The airline recorded $945.2 million as its share of losses from Air India during FY2025/26, contributing to a 56% decline in Singapore Airlines' overall net profit for the year.

Why Air India's Losses Have Ballooned

Air India's financial deterioration stems from multiple operational disruptions beyond its control. Pakistan's ban on Indian carriers using its airspace, imposed in April 2025, forced costly rerouting of long-haul flights. The US-Israeli war with Iran further disrupted international networks. And the fatal crash of an Air India Boeing 787 in June 2025, which killed 260 people, triggered a safety pause that grounded aircraft for inspections and significantly reduced the fleet's capacity.

To manage the bleeding, Air India has cancelled 27% of its international flights — nearly 150 weekly services — between June and August 2026. The Indian rupee's depreciation against the US dollar has added further financial pressure.

Despite the losses, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong, who sits on the Air India board as a non-executive director, has described the investment as a "long game." He noted that Air India's net promoter score has improved by 50 points, citing tangible progress in training, in-flight services, and lounges. SIA has seconded two senior executives to Air India, including a chief operations officer and head of engineering.

Parliamentary Scrutiny Ahead

Tiong has filed a question for oral answer in Singapore's parliament on September 8, asking the transport minister whether losses from and the carrying value of Singapore Airlines' foreign associates have been assessed against its capacity to provide essential transport services. Singapore's Ministry of Transport, Temasek, and Singapore Airlines did not respond to requests for comment.

The political dimension is significant because Temasek, a sovereign wealth fund wholly owned by the Singapore government, is the majority shareholder of Singapore Airlines. While the airline operates commercially and independently, the scale of losses from the Air India investment has prompted questions about whether taxpayer-linked capital is effectively subsidizing a foreign carrier's turnaround.

What It Means for Indian Diaspora Travelers

Air India's transformation under Tata Sons and the partnership with Singapore Airlines is being closely watched by the Indian diaspora, particularly frequent travelers on routes between India and Southeast Asia. Air India CEO Campbell Wilson, who previously headed Singapore Airlines' low-cost carrier Scoot, is leading a five-year turnaround plan. Whether Singapore Airlines maintains or increases its financial commitment will shape the speed and scope of Air India's fleet modernization and service improvements on the long-haul routes that diaspora travelers depend on most.
